The British sacked Oranjestad (Sint Eustatius) in 1781 (Netherlands Antilles page); neither page says it was held. Dutch Sint Maarten's own 1648-1814 history (Spanish, French, British episodes) is not on the pages opened (unverified: page budget).

2,176 km2 in six cells (Curaçao 3, Aruba 1, Bonaire 1, Sint Maarten 1; Saba and Sint Eustatius are too small for the 255 km2 grid): 'From 1815 onwards Curaçao and Dependencies formed a colony of the Kingdom of the Netherlands.' The page's infobox area is 980 km2 before 1986 (Curaçao 444, Bonaire 288, Aruba 180, Sint Maarten 34, Sint Eustatius 21, Saba 13), a ratio of 2.2, the grid's coarseness, not a different extent. 1814 arrangement (Colony page): Curaçao and Dependencies (Curaçao, Aruba, Bonaire) and Sint Eustatius and Dependencies (Sint Eustatius, Sint Maarten, Saba).

region.text: Curaçao, taken by the West India Company fleet

ledger.note: 1634: the Dutch take Curaçao. 'The Dutch West India Company fleet under Admiral Johann van Walbeeck' took the island; it 'invaded the island in 1634' and the Spanish defenders surrendered at San Juan that August. The Colony page's infobox says 'Established: 1634'.
1636: Aruba and Bonaire. 'Curaçao was settled in 1634; Aruba and Bonaire in 1636; Sint Eustatius in 1636; Saba in 1640; Sint Maarten in 1648.' The page does not say who held them before.
1636: Sint Eustatius, its only town Oranjestad later sacked by the British (1781).
1640: Saba.

region.text: the southern part of Saint Martin, the Dutch half

ledger.note: 1648: Saint Martin is divided. 'The island of Saint Martin was split between France and the Netherlands in 1648.' The Dutch half is today's Sint Maarten (34 km2).
1800: the British take Curaçao. 'The British captured Curaçao in 1800 and held it until 1803.'
1803: Curaçao returns to the Dutch after the British three-year hold; 'They attacked again in 1804'.
1807: the second British occupation begins: 'They attacked again in 1804, and then held it from 1807 to 1816.'

1815: 'From 1815 onwards Curaçao and Dependencies formed a colony of the Kingdom of the Netherlands.' The Sint Eustatius, Sint Maarten and Saba group 'became a single Dutch colony in 1815 as Sint Eustatius and Dependencies' (SSS islands page).
1816: the British hand Curaçao back 'under the terms of the Treaty of Paris' (the page cites the 1815 treaty).

region.text: Suriname, merged with Curaçao and Dependencies and Sint Eustatius and Dependencies

ledger.note: 1828: one West Indies colony. 'the three colonies were merged into a single West Indies colony ruled from Paramaribo, Suriname, in 1828.'
1828: the merged colony is governed from Paramaribo, not Willemstad.

1845: Suriname leaves. 'This proved to be an unhappy arrangement, causing it to be partially reverted in 1845.' 'From that year on there were again two West Indian colonies: Suriname, and Curaçao and Dependencies' (History of Curaçao page); Sint Eustatius is ruled from Willemstad.
1845: Willemstad is the capital again; the Dutch part of the SSS islands now belongs to Curaçao and Dependencies, with Willemstad as its capital (SSS islands page).
1936: 'Between 1936 and 1948, the area was officially known as the Territory of Curaçao.'

1948 (May): 'a new constitution for the territory entered into force' and it was 'renamed "Netherlands Antilles"'. On 15 December 1954 the Netherlands Antilles, Suriname and the Netherlands 'acceded as equal partners' in the Kingdom (Charter; infobox gives 10 December).

region.text: Aruba, which 'seceded from the Netherlands Antilles on 1 January 1986'

ledger.note: 1986 (1 January): Aruba becomes a separate country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands, 'status aparte' after a 1977 consultative referendum.
2010 (10 October): Curaçao becomes a country. 'The transition took place at midnight (00:00) on 10 October 2010'; Curaçao and Sint Maarten 'became two new "landen"' within the Kingdom.

region.text: Sint Maarten, a new constituent country

ledger.note: 2010 (10 October): Sint Maarten becomes a country (the Dutch half of Saint Martin).

region.text: Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, which 'have become direct parts of the Netherlands as special municipalities'

ledger.note: 2010 (10 October): the BES islands join the Netherlands as special municipalities. Saba had announced on 1 September 2009 that it wished to withdraw.
2010 (10 October): 'The country was dissolved on 10 October 2010.' Cliopatria keeps a shape to 2024.

wars.name: British occupation of Curaçao
wars.outcome: British captured Curaçao in 1800 and held it until 1803, attacked again in 1804 and held it from 1807 to 1816, returning it under the Treaty of Paris.
wars.note: The page names no battle. The Netherlands Antilles page adds that 'The British sacked its only town, Oranjestad, in 1781' (Sint Eustatius), without saying the island was held.

certainty.note: Small settlements in contested waters (Spain held the surrounding islands); the islands' extent is the island, but the hold on Aruba, Bonaire and Saba is the page's 'settled' only.

Islands bounded by their coasts, and the one land frontier, on Saint Martin (split with France 'in 1648'), is a treaty line. The exception is 1828-1844, when the merged colony included Suriname, whose interior frontiers are soft.

notes: Cliopatria's 'Netherlands Antilles' (1815..2024) is mostly Suriname: the 1820-2023 shapes (149,000 km2) are 524 of Suriname's 539 grid cells plus 12 of Guyana, joined to the six islands; the Netherlands Antilles page says Suriname 'did not become part of the Netherlands Antilles'. The union was real only in the merged West Indies colony of 1828-1845. Dutch Suriname (1667-1975, Dutch from the 1667 Treaty of Breda per the New Netherland page, and a separate colony except 1828-1845) has no row and no dossier: it needs one (suggested slug dutch-suriname); counterpart 'dutch-suriname' here is that slug. The dossier extends the row back to 1634 to carry the islands that Cliopatria filed under New Netherland (1636-1802) and omits for 1803-1814. Successors without rows: Curaçao, Sint Maarten and Aruba (slugs curacao, sint-maarten, aruba used as counterparts; not yet dossiers); Cliopatria's 2024 shape is their land. Saba and Sint Eustatius resolve to no cell on the 255 km2 grid (Natural Earth admin-1 names 'Saba' and 'St. Eustatius', zero cells), so the regions naming them are empty on the grid: that is why the warnings 'region resolves to no cells' appear. Page budget (up to 5): five pages used. Unsettled: who held Aruba, Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba before the Dutch, Sint Maarten's Spanish and French interludes, the 1781-1784 Sint Eustatius episode, the 1845-1954 internal reorganisations, the 1983 split of the SSS islands into three territories, the 15 versus 10 December 1954 Charter date (body versus infobox).
